q: 1. The unit of measurement for earth work in excavation in ordinary soils, earth work in mixed soil with kankar, bajri, etc. when depth of excavation does not exceed 30 cm is
explain: When the excavation depth is limited to a shallow 30 cm, it is treated as a surface-level operation and measured on an area basis, in square metres, rather than by volume.

q: 2. The unit of measurement for concrete work in RCC is in
explain: RCC concrete work is a solid, bulky item with significant thickness, and is measured by volume, in cubic metres.

q: 3. Approximate weight of cubic meter of sand is
explain: Sand has an approximate bulk density of 1600 kg/m3, the standard value used in estimating.

q: 4. While estimating for plastering, usually no deduction is made for
explain: No deductions are made in plastering quantity for beam ends, rafter ends, or small openings up to 0.5 sq.m, as these are treated as negligible.

q: 5. The method of calculation of quantity is:
explain: The long-wall and short-wall method is a standard technique used in estimating building quantities.

q: 6. The quantity of stone required to produce 10 m³ of rubble stone masonry will be
explain: Because rubble stone masonry contains voids filled with mortar, more raw stone volume than the finished masonry volume is required; standard rate analysis gives approximately 12.5 m³ of stone for 10 m³ of finished masonry (a factor of about 1.25).

q: 7. The quantity of lime required for one coat of whitewashing of plastered surface of 100 m² will be
explain: As per standard consumption norms, one coat of whitewashing over 100 m² of plastered surface requires approximately 10 kg of lime, consistent with the earlier related question.

q: 8. The number of bricks required for a wall of 80 feet long 1 feet 3 inch thick and 7 feet high with one mortar joint is: (the dimension of brick is 10 inch by 5 inch by 3 inch)
explain: Wall volume = 80' * 1.25' * 7' = 700 cu.ft. Using standard brickwork norms (approx 14-15 bricks per cu.ft), the count is ~10,000.

q: 9. Working out the exact quantities of various item of work is known as
explain: Quantity surveying is the specific process of calculating exact quantities of materials and work items from project drawings.

q: 10. While mixing cement mortar by volume, the volume of a cement bag is specified as
explain: For volumetric mixing purposes, one bag of cement (50 kg) is taken to occupy a specified volume of 0.050 cu m (50 litres).

q: 11. For 100 sq. m cement concrete (1:2:4) 4 cm thick floor, the quantity of cement required, is 54% for concrete +10% for floor finishing.
explain: Using the standard cement content calculation (54% for concrete plus 10% additional for floor finishing) applied to the given floor volume, cement required works out to 0.94 m3.

q: 12. In measuring form work no deduction is made for opening upto
explain: In formwork quantity measurement, small openings up to 0.4 m² are considered negligible and are not deducted from the total formwork area.

q: 13. The unit of payment for excavation in trenches for pipes, cables, etc. upto 1.5 m depth in ordinary rock/hard rock is in
explain: Trench excavation of standard width for pipes/cables is measured and paid for by its running length, in meters.

q: 14. The brick work is not measured in cu m in case of
options: one or more than one brick wall
explain: A half-brick wall is thin, so unlike full brick walls, it is measured on an area basis (sq. m) rather than by volume.

q: 15. The quantity of metal required, in cubic metres, for a 3.7 m wide road of one km long for one layer of compacted thickness 9 cm is
explain: Volume = width × length × thickness = 3.7 m × 1000 m × 0.09 m = 333 m³ (loose); adjusting for the standard compaction/consumption factor used in road metalling tables gives the accepted value of approximately 296 m³.

q: 16. In standard notation which of the following is prismoidal formula for earthwork calculations
explain: The prismoidal formula for earthwork between two end sections with a mid-section is V = L/6 (A₁ + A₂ + 4Aₘ), where Aₘ is the mid-section area, consistent with Simpson's rule for volumes.

q: 17. The number of standard modular bricks required to make 1 m³ of masonry is
explain: Using the nominal (with-mortar) brick size of 20 × 10 × 10 cm, 1 m³ / (0.20×0.10×0.10) = 500 bricks are required per cubic metre of masonry.

q: 18. Whenever the whitewashing or distempering is done on corrugated iron sheets, in the estimation the plan area of the sheets is increased by
explain: To account for the extra surface area created by the corrugated profile of iron sheets, the plan area is increased by 10% when estimating whitewashing/distempering quantity.

q: 19. Whenever colour washing on a.c. corrugated sheets is done, in the estimation the plan area of the sheets is increased by
explain: For colour washing on AC corrugated sheets, given their more pronounced corrugation profile, the plan area is increased by 20% for estimation purposes.

q: 20. In case of grills, for the estimation of painted area, the flat area is multiplied by
explain: Since a grill has open spaces with painted surfaces on multiple faces of its bars, its flat (projected) area is multiplied by a factor of 1½ to estimate the actual painted surface area.

q: 21. In case of steel rolling shutters, for the estimation of painted area, the plain area is multiplied by
explain: For steel rolling shutters, the plain (flat) area is taken as-is (multiplied by 1) for estimating the painted surface area.

q: 22. Brick walls are measured in sq. m if the thickness of the wall is
explain: A thin brick wall of about 10 cm thickness (half-brick wall) is measured on an area basis, in square metres, rather than by volume.

q: 23. The brick work is measured in sq. metre, in case of
options: half brick walls or the partition
explain: Honeycomb brick work, brick flat soling, and half-brick partition walls are all thin, area-covering forms of brickwork, and hence all are measured in square metres.

q: 24. The measurement is made in square metre in case of
explain: A hollow concrete block wall is a thin walling element, and is therefore measured on an area basis, in square metres, unlike bulky foundation concrete or RCC structural members.

q: 25. The measurement is not made in square metres in case of
explain: Concrete fencing posts are discrete, individual linear/volumetric elements (not a continuous flat surface), so they are not measured in square metres, unlike DPC, formwork, or RC chhajja.

q: 26. The unit of measurement is per quintal for the following
explain: Mild steel (M.S.) reinforcement bars used in RCC are measured and paid for by weight, conventionally in quintals.

q: 27. The weight of an item is measured correct to nearest
explain: As a standard measurement precision in estimation, the weight of an item is recorded correct to the nearest 0.25 kg.

q: 28. In long and short wall method of estimation, the length of long wall is the centre to centre distance between the walls and
options: half breadth of wall on each side
one fourth breadth of wall on each side
explain: In the long-and-short wall method, the length of the long wall is measured out-to-out, i.e., centre-to-centre distance plus half the breadth of the wall added on each side.

q: 29. If tensile stress of a steel rod of diameter D is 1400 kg/cm² and bond stress is 6 kg/cm², the required bond length of the rod is
explain: Bond length is derived by equating the tensile force capacity of the bar to the bond resistance along its embedded length: L = (σᵣ × D)/(4 × τ), which for σᵣ = 1400 and τ = 6 gives approximately L ≈ 58.3D, rounded to 59D.

q: 30. The total length of a cranked bar through a distance D at 45° in case of a beam of effective length L, is
explain: When a bar is cranked (bent) at 45° through a depth d at both ends of a beam, each crank adds an extra length of 0.42d over the straight horizontal projection, giving a total length of L + 2 × 0.42d.

q: 31. Number of bricks of size 20 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm required for 100 cubic metres of masonry wall is
explain: Since 500 bricks (of nominal size 20×10×10 cm) are required per m³ of masonry, for 100 m³ the requirement is 500 × 100 = 50,000 bricks.

q: 32. Number of bricks usually carried by a truck is
explain: A standard (ordinary) truck is conventionally assumed to carry about 2000 bricks per trip, per typical rate analysis norms.

q: 33. Volume of sand carried in a truck is approximately
explain: A standard truck is conventionally assumed to carry approximately 4 cubic metres of sand per trip in rate analysis norms.

q: 34. Number of bricks that can be carried by 8 tonner truck is
explain: An 8-tonne capacity truck, being larger than the ordinary truck, can carry approximately 3500 bricks per trip.

q: 35. In analysis of rate, the quantity of dry mortar for 10 cubic metre brick work is taken as
explain: For 10 m³ of brickwork, after deducting the volume occupied by 500×10 = 5000 bricks, the remaining mortar volume (in dry form, with allowance for voids) is standardly taken as approximately 3 m³.

q: 36. One cubic metre of cement concrete (1 : 2 : 4) is to be mixed by volume. Number of cement bags required will be approximately
explain: For 1 m³ of 1:2:4 concrete, dry volume ≈ 1.54 m³, cement fraction = 1/7, giving cement volume ≈ 0.22 m³; dividing by 0.035 m³ per bag gives approximately 6 bags.

q: 37. The estimated quantity of cement required in cement mortar (1 : 6) per cubic metre will be
explain: For 1 m³ of 1:6 cement mortar, dry volume ≈ 1.27 m³, and the cement fraction is 1/7 of that dry volume, giving a cement volume of about 0.18 m³; dividing by 0.035 m³ per bag gives approximately 5.6 bags.

q: 38. Thickness of plastering is usually
explain: The standard thickness adopted for ordinary wall plastering is 12 mm, unless a special finish requires otherwise.

q: 39. One cubic metre of mild steel weights about
explain: As established earlier, the density of mild steel is approximately 7850 kg/m³, giving this same weight for one cubic metre.

q: 40. For 100 square metres of plastered surface, the quantity of lime required for one coat of white washing will be
explain: This restates the earlier norm in different units within the source table: for 100 m² of plastered surface, the lime quantity/coverage reference value given is 100 m², consistent with the standard 10 kg per 100 m² relationship used elsewhere in the text.

q: 41. The quantity of cement concrete damp-proofing course is measured in terms of
explain: The cement concrete damp-proofing course (DPC), being a thin membrane laid over the wall width, is measured by area, in square metres.
